newsitem.title: USA: Greenpeace seeks ban on PVC plastics.
newsitem.headline: Greenpeace seeks ban on PVC plastics.

text.p: Greenpeace Tuesday issued reports they say link cancer-causing dioxins to polyvinyl chloride plastics used in products such as shower curtains, toys, household pipes and medical supplies.

PVCs, identified by the number "3" on recyclable plastics, are an $18-billion-a-year global industry and are the second most widely used type of plastic in the world, according to the chemical industry.

The Greenpeace reports claim that dioxins, known toxins that are as much as 200,000 times more carcinogenic than the pesticide DDT, are released in the production of PVC and when PVC is burned in waste incinerators and accidental fires.
"We want to eliminate PVC as a chlorinated plastic," said Rick Hind, a legislative director with Greenpeace.
Industry groups counter that that current levels of dioxin are at the lowest in 25 years, even though the production of PVC has tripled.
"That clearly shows there is no link between dioxin in the environment and PVC production," said Kip Howlett, vice president of the Chlorine Industry Council.
Howlett said wastewater from PVC plants have shown no measurable releases of dioxin and that samples taken by Greenpeace for its reports were at the midpoint of the manufacturing process.
"In fact, those wastes are treated as part of the process, and the dioxins are either totally destroyed or they're converted into innocuous byproducts," Howlett said.

Greenpeace said it is focusing on PVC because it is the world's fastest growing use of industrial chlorine, a chemical that the pulp and paper industry switched from as a bleach in the late 1980s because of environmental protest.
Hind said Dow Chemical Co is the world's largest producer of chlorine.
Greenpeace claims it has already won a delay in the construction of an $800 million plant being built in Louisiana by Shintech Inc, a subsidiary of Japan's Shin-Etsu Chemical Co Ltd.
Other leading manufacturers of PVC include Dow, Borden Chemicals Inc, Taiwan's Formosa Plastics Corp, Geon Co, Georgia Gulf Corp and Occidental Petroleum Corp.

William Carroll, a spokesman for the Vinyl Institute, which released its own study claiming to disprove a link between PVC incineration and dioxin, said historically the use of PVCs have grown at a rate greater than the growth rate of the world's gross domestic product.

Carroll, who is also vice president of chlorovinyl issues for Occidental Chemical in Dallas, said PVC plastics are widely used for products such as hospital gloves, blood bags, home siding and other goods because of its flexibility, durability and strength.
He said Occidental Chemcial is expanding PVC production at two of its plants in Texas.
"This material has a very bright future," Carroll said. "The reports I've seen are an unwarranted attack on a very good and useful material, and ultimately they'll be seen for that."
